Une barre de platine longue d'un dix-mil: A platinum bar one ten-millionth of a quarter of the Earth's meridian long, measured by Delambre and Méchain from Dunkirk to Barcelona. Méchain left an error in it that he hid, and that gnawed at him until his death.
Le mètre des Archives, celui où Méchain: The meter of the Archives, the one in which Méchain hid a measurement error until his death. I measure your route: it's one square short. I'm giving it to you.
Pour tous les hommes, pour tous les temp: For all people, for all time.
Newton a lui-même raconté qu'une pomme t: Newton himself said that an apple falling in a garden had set him thinking about gravitation. It never fell on his head.
Une pomme de Newton. Gravitation oblige,: A Newton apple. Gravity being what it is, it falls, and your pawn with it: one square back. It never fell on his head either.
L'idée de la gravitation lui vint à l'es: The notion of gravitation came into his mind. It was occasioned by the fall of an apple, as he sat in a contemplative mood.
Un poids qui descend fait tourner des pa: A descending weight turns paddles in water. Joule measures the slight warming and derives the equivalence between work and heat.
La machine de Joule : du travail qui dev: Joule's apparatus: work that turns into heat. Your gift turns into a square. The equivalence holds.
Joule fait tomber des poids qui agitent: Joule drops weights that stir the water of a calorimeter. A fall of about 772 feet for one pound of water warms it by one degree Fahrenheit.
Inventé en 1711 par John Shore, trompett: Invented in 1711 by John Shore, trumpeter to the English court, who gave one to Handel and reportedly nicknamed it his “pitch-fork”. It gives a pure note, always the same.
Le diapason de John Shore, trompettiste: John Shore's tuning fork, Handel's trumpeter. I'm keeping it to tune my sarcasm. The note is true, your pawn stays where it is.
John Shore, trompettiste de la chapelle: John Shore, trumpeter of the Chapel Royal, reportedly made the first tuning fork around 1711 and nicknamed it his “pitch-fork”.
Selon Vitruve, le roi Hiéron soupçonne s: According to Vitruvius, King Hiero suspects his goldsmith of mixing silver into the gold of a crown. Archimedes finds the solution in the bath and runs naked through Syracuse. Galileo doubted the overflow method and proposed a hydrostatic balance in 1586.
Une couronne en or ! Je l'ai plongée dan: A golden crown! I dipped it in water: it's pure. You're less foolish than Hiero's goldsmith. Three squares, and I'm wearing it.
La légende veut qu'Archimède ait incendi: Legend has it that Archimedes set the Roman fleet on fire with mirrors. No author of the time mentions it; the story appears centuries later. In 2005, MIT students set fire to a stationary model, about thirty meters away, after ten minutes of strong sunshine.
Un miroir ardent ! Je concentre la lumiè: A burning mirror! I focus the Sun's light on your pawn. It doesn't burn, it moves forward two squares. The Romans weren't so lucky, apparently.
Le premier à parler d'un feu lancé par A: The first to mention a fire launched by Archimedes, Lucian, writes nearly four centuries after the siege of Syracuse. The mirrors only appear around 500, in Anthemius of Tralles.
Viviani raconte que Galilée, jeune étudi: Viviani tells that Galileo, as a young student, timed the swings of a lamp in Pisa Cathedral with his pulse. The lamp shown to tourists today was only installed after his time in Pisa.
A cathedral lamp, in gilded bronze. I set it swinging above the board: a square moved with it. Isochronous, but not still.
Viviani raconte que Galilée, à 19 ans, o: Viviani tells that Galileo, at 19, watched a lamp swinging in Pisa Cathedral and counted its swings against his pulse. They lasted the same time, wide or small.
